paras: The lynching of Hume Redman took place in Evansville, Indiana, early on October 11, 1882, when about 100 armed men from Posey County broke into the county jail, took out Redman, who was accused of killing his wife, and killed him in the street. Police fired on the retreating mob, and one of its members, David Murphy, was also killed. Papers across the country carried the story as a street battle between officers and lynchers, and several editors defended the killing of Redman.

According to an Evansville dispatch, neighbors of Redman, who lived about three miles from Mount Vernon in Posey County, heard a woman's cries for mercy, blows and a pistol shot on a Friday night, followed by Redman's voice asking, in the dispatch's words, whether he had hit "Eva." Redman called the neighbors and said his wife had shot herself, but she died soon after they found her on the floor with a derringer in her lap. The Boonville Standard said Redman had come home drunk, that the woman's body showed bruises and knife cuts, and that his suicide claim "does not take at all."

Redman was jailed, and the first dispatches reported about 200 armed men around the jail "seeking an opportunity to lynch him." Because a party was forming to lynch him, he was moved from the Mount Vernon jail to Evansville. One brief added that he had served a term in the Illinois penitentiary for homicide.

On the afternoon and night of October 10, men came up from Mount Vernon by train and on horseback, met near Salt Wells, and started for the jail at 2 a.m. A telephone warning from Ullmer's brewery reached Night Turnkey Hatmacher at 2:10, and Sheriff Keath, his deputies and Detective Newitt prepared to defend the jail. The mob picketed its horses, captured passersby and the sheriff, and broke the jail doors with sledge hammers and chisels while officers and attackers exchanged shots.

The men tied Redman's hands and brought him out, their leader answering an order to halt: "We are from Posey Co., and came after Redman, and we are going to have him." A chemical fire engine answering the alarm struck and overturned the buggy holding Redman, and the leaders, after first calling to put him on horseback, ordered him killed on the spot. One man struck him on the head with a sledge hammer, and the Globe's dispatch reported that over two dozen balls entered his body where he fell on Third Street.

Police, firing without orders, fought the retreating mob along Third Street, and Chief Pritchell and Newitt were pinned to the ground by return fire. David Murphy, a Mount Vernon man described as the murdered woman's brother-in-law, fell from his horse half a square away and died in the courthouse, where Redman's body had also been taken.

Police arrested Quincy A. Gill near the bodies, Dave McFadden, called a brother of the murdered woman, in Young's saloon, and a horseman who fired at officers. On October 13 the grand jury indicted Gill, Floyd and McFadden for conspiracy, and they were released on $1,000 bond each, with Posey County bondsmen. Four other wounded raiders were reported in poor condition, and no report of an inquest or a trial appears in the coverage.

At Mount Vernon, 500 people attended Murphy's funeral, a fund was raised for a monument and his three orphans, and Posey County residents were reported indignant at his death. Evansville officers guarded the prisoners against a feared second mob.

The story ran in white papers from Washington to Sacramento within a day, first as a short wire that guessed Redman had been hanged on the Mount Vernon road and then as a long Evansville dispatch. Headlines varied from the St. Paul Globe's "Handsomely Lynched" to the Memphis Appeal's "A Pitched Battle," and weekly summaries repeated the account into late October. No paper read named Redman's race or used racial language about the case.

Much comment excused the lynching: the Memphis Public Ledger called Redman's crime "one of the most atrocious" ever committed, the Carson City Morning Appeal said a wife-beater deserved "the riddling shower of bullets," and the Boonville Standard called his death "too good for him." The Savannah Morning News instead praised the Indiana police as "creditable to Northern civilization" while calling the lynchers' conduct the reverse, and a Vermont weekly said lynch law had "resulted very sadly."

The first wires said police fire killed Murphy, while the fuller dispatch and a later comment held that the mob fired through its own ranks. Accounts also differ on whether Redman died from the hammer blow alone or from gunfire as well, on whether Murphy was the woman's brother-in-law or brother, and on whether the attack came at midnight Tuesday or 2 a.m. Wednesday.

bases: About 100 men from Posey County broke into the Evansville jail, took out Hume Redman, accused of killing his wife, and killed him in the street (A5, A12, A30).

A mob of about 100 armed men took Redman from the county jail over the resistance of the sheriff and police and killed him with a sledge hammer blow (and, by one account, gunfire) because he was accused of murdering his wife (A5, A12, A34). No paper read states Redman's race or the mob's.
Independent dispatches and the regional Boonville Standard agree on the jail break, Redman's killing in the street and Murphy's death (A5, A12, A34), though details of how both died differ (A4, A12).

accounts.label: First Evansville wire
accounts.gist: The mob took Redman out in a buggy toward the Mount Vernon road and was supposed to have hanged him; police fire killed Dave Murphy.

accounts.label: Full Evansville dispatch
accounts.gist: After a fire engine overturned the buggy, the mob killed Redman on the spot with a sledge hammer, over two dozen balls entered his body, and Murphy was likely hit by the mob's own fire.

accounts.label: Boonville (Ind.) Standard
accounts.gist: Redman, a drinker, beat and shot his wife; when police came up a mob member felled him with the sledge, killing him instantly; Murphy died in the retreat.

accounts.label: Wire news summary
accounts.gist: A mob member, fearing the rescue of Redman, killed him with a sledge hammer as citizens collected by the police chief attacked the mob.

framing.detail: The St. Paul Globe headlined 'Strung Up' and 'Handsomely Lynched' and wrote of hemp 'long ago prepared for him.'
The Memphis Appeal ran the long dispatch as 'A Pitched Battle' between officers and 'a Determined Mob.'
The Memphis Public Ledger called Redman guilty of 'one of the most atrocious crimes ever perpetrated' and his killing an execution by a mob.
The Savannah Morning News praised the Northern police and condemned the lynchers as a sectional jab.
The Carson City Morning Appeal said a wife-beater deserved nothing less than 'the riddling shower of bullets.'
The Boonville Standard called the sledge blow 'a death too good for him' and blamed the liquor traffic.
The Orleans County Monitor said 'Lynch law resulted very sadly.'

The Memphis Appeal of Oct 13 also places Murphy's death 'Tuesday night' (A19).
'Perry' is likely a slip for Posey.
